title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Problem Statement



RKR is moving from an instructional restaurant to a dual model that adds stand-alone service days (Kwok 2026).
Stand-alone days cannot rely on state funding, so they need steady reservations to stay viable (Kwok 2026).
The Collins Concierge already reaches faculty and staff, the segment that best fits RKR’s weekday lunch hours (The Restaurant at Kellogg Ranch n.d.).



The gap
The RKR section is mostly text, and the “Reserve a Table” button sits at the bottom, below the hours.1 Readers who skim can scroll past it.



The business problem comes straight from Dr. Kwok’s proposal: the stand-alone service days need their own demand. The newsletter is the cheapest place to start because RKR already owns it and the audience is already on campus. The issue is the design: text heavy, button at the bottom.

Based on the team’s review of current Concierge issues, Fall 2026.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Analytics Objective

PO1: Strengthen the visual design of RKR’s section of The Collins Concierge to drive reservation growth.



AO1: Compare RKR click rates and attributed OpenTable reservations across RKR newsletter section designs, testing button placement in Fall 2026 and image versus video in Spring 2027.



Fall 2026 Move “Reserve a Table” to the upper left, compared with past issues
Spring 2027 A/B test image vs. video, with the button fixed in the upper left

One change at a time. Fall isolates placement. Spring isolates media. If both changed at once, there would be no way to tell which one moved clicks.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Importance



Reaches the primary segment
Faculty and staff rated highest in the team’s segment analysis, and the Concierge reaches them directly.


Low cost, already owned
No ad spend. The section runs every week, so each issue is a chance to test.


Measurable end to end
Canva tracks views and clicks; version-specific links can tie clicks to OpenTable bookings.



One change
at a time.




Clicks show interest, not bookings. Reservations remain the secondary, validating measure (Kumar 2021).

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Well-established Models








Framework
Key finding
What it means for AO1




Email response process
Newsletter response moves from seeing, to engaging, to acting; format tests against a control work well (Hartemo, Suomi, and Hakala 2016)
Use past issues as the control baseline


Relational vs. transactional metrics
Across 811 newsletters, clicks had the strongest link to eventual purchase (Kumar 2021)
Click-through rate is the primary metric


Visual heuristics
Readers scan newsletters in a U-shape; upper-left links earn higher CTR (Kumar and Salo 2018)
Fall moves the button to the upper left


Visual attention
Large images drew more attention than prices or codes, and attention mapped to purchase (Skourou and Spiliotopoulos 2024)
Spring tests image vs. video


Cognitive load
GIFs and emojis together raised unsubscribes, though neither hurt CTR alone (Bashirzadeh, Mai, and Faure 2022)
Add only one visual element at a time




Industry guides from Semrush and OpenTable point the same way: key information and a bold button near the top, strong food photos, and test one variable at a time over at least two weeks.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Challenges in the Literature



Inbox overload
University recipients reported about 30 bulk emails a week and trashed 22% of newsletters (Kong, Zhu, and Konstan 2021). Academics at one business school received 324 organizational bulk emails in a year (Bicudo De Castro 2025).



Email needs a clear role
Readers resisted email that did not fit their customer journey (Zunac, Miletic, and Kozina 2022).




Implication: A redesign may not move CTR if readers never reach the RKR section. AO1 tracks views alongside clicks to separate a design problem from a readership problem.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Adequacy of the Information


Strengths

Covers attention, button placement, media, and fatigue
Findings line up with industry guidance (Go 2024; Jones 2023)
Directly actionable for a newsletter section


Limitations

Industry guides come from companies selling services
The eye-tracking study had a small sample (Skourou and Spiliotopoulos 2024)
The email-role study was mostly female participants (Zunac, Miletic, and Kozina 2022)




The gap: No reviewed study looks at a restaurant section inside a university newsletter. Primary data from the Concierge fills it.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Need for Additional Analysis

Build a baseline of RKR click rates from past Concierge issues in Canva.
Fall 2026: measure the effect of moving the button to the upper left.
Spring 2027: alternate image and video issues weekly, button fixed.
Tag links by version so OpenTable bookings trace back to the design.
Flag unusual weeks such as holidays, finals, and campus events.


Clicks will not capture everyone. Walk-in guests and Bronco Bucks payers may never click, so a “How did you hear about us?” question at booking helps account for those visits.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Data and Sampling



Source: Canva website insights for The Collins Concierge, exported as one CSV per issue
Window: the last 12 weeks of issues
Sampling: all available issues in the window (non-probability, convenience)
Cleaning: 14 exports received; 1 byte-identical duplicate removed, leaving 13 issues




2,681


total page views across 13 issues





The “Reserve a Table” button links to the RKR website rather than straight to OpenTable, so clicks to cpp.edu/rkr pages are the measurable step before a booking.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Data Wrangling
Each export stacks four dimensions (country, device, source, link) in long format. The code below collapses them to one row per issue.

issue_summary <- issues |>
  group_by(issue) |>
  summarise(
    views       = sum(Count[Dimension == "country"]),
    mobile      = sum(Count[Dimension == "device" & Name == "Mobile"]),
    link_clicks = sum(Count[Dimension == "link"]),
    rkr_clicks  = sum(Count[Dimension == "link" &
                            str_detect(Name, "cpp\\.edu/rkr")]),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(ctr = rkr_clicks / views)


Lines 1 and 2: start from the stacked data and group by issue. Line 4: views come from the country rows, which sum to total page views. Lines 7 and 8: RKR clicks are any link to cpp.edu/rkr, which covers both the homepage and the menu page. Line 10: click rate is RKR clicks divided by views.

section: Baseline: RKR Click Rate by Issue
text:
Baseline: RKR Click Rate by Issue


This is the pre-test baseline that Fall’s button move will be compared against. Clicks to RKR are low across the board, which is exactly the problem AO1 is designed to address.

title: Newsletter Design and Reservation Growth
text:
Analytics Methods


A/B testing in two phases
Only one element changes per phase, so any difference in clicks can be traced to that change.
Two-proportion z-test
Compares click rates between conditions at α = 0.05:
\[z = \frac{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2}{\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}}\]


Independent-samples t-test
Compares the average weekly OpenTable reservations attributed to each design.


Why these methods

The z-test is the standard way to compare two rates
The t-test fits weekly reservation counts across two groups
Together they follow the reader’s path from view → click → booking (Hartemo, Suomi, and Hakala 2016)

text:
Data Notes

Files: 14 Canva CSV exports in data/concierge-canva/, one per issue
Duplicates: 1 export was byte-identical to another and was removed with an MD5 check
Issue order: files are sorted by their export timestamp, which follows publication order
RKR clicks: any link containing cpp.edu/rkr; no direct OpenTable links appear in the exports
Views: sum of country rows, which matches total page views reported by Canva
Not yet available: issue dates, the first issue with the upper-left button, and OpenTable reservations by link
